title: Hard edge, soft spine
question: How Was a Medieval Sword Actually Made?
scoredBy: inspection of rendered frames at 0/33/66/94 per shot
verdict: The best-looking typography of the five and still a process film with no process in it. Forging is a sequence -- heat, fold, quench, and the differential cooling that is the whole design -- and a sequence is the one thing this reel cannot draw. What it does have is the cleanest type: the gold-heat spotlight gives the frame a centre, and 'Iron / with too / LITTLE / carbon / bends' set at 170px across five lines is a real composition rather than a caption.
whatWorked: Typography at its best in this benchmark: five short lines at statement scale, serif against heavy sans, one accent word, the rest getting out of the way.
The spotlight field gives the frame an optical centre, which the wash field does not.
The script's structure is textbook: what it is not, the constraint, the dilemma, the solution, the method, the trick, and the counter-example that proves it.
Highest motion-design score of the five (10/10) -- every shot obeys the two-events rule.

whatFailed.what: Not one of heat, folding, quenching or differential cooling is shown.
whatFailed.why: A forging sequence needs a process representation. The five diagram types cover a mechanism, a span of years, a magnitude, an orbit and a scan.

whatFailed.what: 'Twelve hundred degrees' did not become a measurement bar.
whatFailed.why: The MAGNITUDE regex lists tons, miles, metres, feet, pounds and people. Degrees is not a unit it knows, so the one line in the episode with a drawable figure fell to typography.

whatFailed.what: A wire prop and the slate share the opening frame's single beat.

whatFailed.why: The camera quota counts across the reel but cannot refuse a run when the beat pool for three adjacent shots resolves the same way.

gatesFailed: no photograph anywhere in the reel — every shot is drawn or typeset
